name: Ibis
vendor: Ibis project (core team sponsored by Voltron Data)
summary: A Python dataframe API that compiles to SQL, so the same code runs on DuckDB on a laptop and on BigQuery, Snowflake, PostgreSQL or more than 20 other engines.
intro: Ibis looks like a dataframe library: you `filter`, `group_by`, `agg`, `join` and `order_by` tables in Python. But nothing runs when you write those lines. Ibis builds a lazy expression, and only an action such as `to_pandas()`, `to_pyarrow()` or `to_polars()` sends it to a backend. For most backends Ibis compiles the expression to that engine’s SQL dialect with SQLGlot; the rest are DataFrame backends that get the engine’s own native calls. `ibis.to_sql(expr)` shows the SQL, and `table.sql("...")` mixes hand-written SQL into a pipeline.

The backend is chosen by the connection, such as `ibis.duckdb.connect()` or `ibis.bigquery.connect(...)`, so the idea is to develop against a local file and deploy against the warehouse by changing one line. DuckDB is the default and recommended backend for local data. The list includes DataFusion, Druid, Flink, Impala, PySpark, Athena, BigQuery, ClickHouse, Databricks, DuckDB, Exasol, Materialize, MySQL, Oracle, Polars, PostgreSQL, RisingWave, SingleStoreDB, SQL Server, SQLite, Snowflake and Trino. Because the target is SQL, Ibis follows SQL semantics: tables have no index and no guaranteed row order. Google’s BigQuery DataFrames, a pandas-style API, is built on Ibis.
strengths: One API for more than 20 engines: prototype on DuckDB or Polars with a sample, then point the same code at BigQuery, Snowflake or Trino
Interactive mode for exploring data step by step, with the same expressions reused in pipeline code
Composes with SQL instead of hiding it: inspect the generated SQL with `ibis.to_sql`, or start from a SQL query and continue in Python
Reads CSV and Parquet files directly through the backend, e.g. `con.read_parquet(...)` on DuckDB, Polars or DataFusion
limits: Not a drop-in pandas replacement: no index, no positional access and no guaranteed row order, so pandas code needs rewriting
Not every operation works on every backend; Ibis publishes an operation support matrix, and portable code sticks to the common subset
Breaking changes across major versions: 9.0 (May 2024) replaced SQLAlchemy with SQLGlot internally, and 10.0 (February 2025) removed the pandas and Dask backends
Its own docs say Voltron Data is the primary sponsor and employs most of the core team, so the project depends heavily on one company

story: Wes McKinney, the creator of pandas, started Ibis in 2015 as a pandas-like interface to Apache Impala. The first release on PyPI was 0.3.0 in July 2015.

The project grew from one engine to many. For years it had no default backend, because nobody on the team was comfortable making pandas, the only in-memory engine at the time, the default. DuckDB changed that: it handles larger-than-memory CSV, Parquet and JSON files, and became the recommended backend for local data. Under the stewardship of Phillip Cloud and a team employed by Voltron Data, which McKinney co-founded, Ibis 9.0 in May 2024 finished “the big refactor” from SQLAlchemy to SQLGlot, and Ibis 10.0 in February 2025 removed the pandas and Dask backends. Version 12.0 followed in February 2026.

choices.why: A deferred expression can be compiled and shipped to the engine that holds the data. pandas computes each step as you go, which is why the Ibis team said making it behave in a deferred way was hard and eventually dropped it as a backend.
Most data engines speak SQL and many have no Python API. Generating each engine’s dialect lets one Python API reach all of them, and since 9.0 SQLGlot does the dialect work.

Ibis has no index and makes no promise about row order, because, as its pandas guide puts it, SQL “makes no guarantees about row order”. Ibis tables follow the same rules as the database tables they stand for.
DuckDB offered “the uber-convenience of SQLite but for analytic use cases” and handles larger-than-memory CSV, Parquet and JSON files, so it became the recommended way to work with local data.

timeline.text: Wes McKinney starts Ibis for Apache Impala; 0.3.0 on PyPI in July
Ibis 9.0 in May completes the move from SQLAlchemy to SQLGlot
Ibis 10.0 in February removes the pandas and Dask backends
